chapter.name: A Journey through States of Water

questions.q: What is the process called in which water changes into its vapour state?
questions.a: Evaporation: the process of conversion of water into its vapour state is called evaporation.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of evaporation?
o: Wet hair becoming dry some time after a bath
An ice cube turning into water in a cup
Drops forming on the outside of a cold bottle
Coconut oil turning solid on a winter night
questions.a: Wet hair becoming dry some time after a bath: the water on the hair changes into water vapour and goes into the air.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): We cannot see the water vapour that leaves a wet cloth drying on a line.
Reason (R): Water vapour is invisible; steam looks visible only because it holds tiny droplets of water.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: water vapour itself is invisible, so the vapour leaving the cloth cannot be seen.

questions.q:
Read the statements about evaporation.
I. Evaporation takes place continuously, even at room temperature.
II. Steam above a hot dosa pan looks white because water vapour itself is white.
III. If the underside of a steel plate stays dry while the water on top disappears, the water has not seeped through the plate.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only: evaporation goes on even at room temperature, and a dry underside shows that no water seeped through; II is wrong because water vapour is invisible and steam looks white only because of the tiny water droplets in it.

questions.q: Define evaporation. Give one example of evaporation from daily life.
questions.a: Evaporation is the process of conversion of water into its vapour state. Example: wet clothes drying on a line (or a mopped floor drying, or sweat drying on the body).
s: Correct definition: water changing into its vapour state
One correct everyday example, such as wet clothes drying

questions.q: True or False? Wet clothes hung inside a room on a cool, cloudy day still lose water to the air by evaporation, even though nobody heats them. Give a reason.
questions.a: True. Evaporation takes place continuously, even at room temperature, so the water in the clothes keeps changing into water vapour and going into the air; heating is not needed.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: evaporation goes on continuously even at room temperature, without heating

questions.q:
Answer each part in one line.
(a) Is water vapour a solid, a liquid or a gas?
(b) Where does the water from a mopped floor go when the floor dries?
(c) Water vapour is present in the air around us. Can we see it?
questions.a: (a) A gas: water vapour is the gaseous state of water. (b) It changes into water vapour and goes into the air around us. (c) No: water vapour is invisible to us.
s: (a) Gas (gaseous state)
(b) Into the air around us as water vapour
(c) No, it is invisible

questions.q:
Ravi writes his homework with a fountain pen that uses watery ink. He must wait a little before closing his notebook, or the ink smudges on the facing page.
(a) What happens to the water in the ink while Ravi waits?
(b) On a humid, rainy day he has to wait longer than usual. Why?
(c) His teacher says the ink would dry sooner if he gently waved the open notebook. Why would this help?
questions.a: (a) The water in the ink evaporates: it changes into water vapour and goes into the air, so the ink becomes dry. (b) On a rainy day the air is more humid: it already holds a lot of water vapour, so the water in the ink evaporates more slowly. (c) Waving moves the air over the page, and with more movement of air, water evaporates faster.
s: (a) The water evaporates into the air as water vapour
(b) The air is humid (already holds much water vapour), so evaporation is slower
(c) Moving air makes water evaporate faster

questions.q:
In a science period in Guwahati, a group pours 100 mL of water into each of two paper cups of the same size: one is coated with wax on the inside, the other is plain paper with no coating. Each cup stands in its own dry steel tray, side by side on the same bench. By the end of the school day the waxed cup holds 94 mL and its tray is dry. The plain cup holds 68 mL, its outside is soggy, and 24 mL of water has collected in its tray.
(a) Through which cup did water seep? Give the evidence.
(b) By which process did the waxed cup lose its water? How do you know?
(c) How much water did the plain cup lose in all?
(d) Riya says, 'All the water that the plain cup lost is now in its tray.' Judge her claim, showing your working.
questions.a: (a) The plain cup: water collected in the tray under it, while the tray under the waxed cup stayed dry. (b) Evaporation: the water changed into water vapour and went into the air; none seeped out, because its tray stayed dry. (c) 100 - 68 = 32 mL. (d) She is wrong: the tray holds only 24 mL, so 32 - 24 = 8 mL is neither in the cup nor in the tray; that water went into the air as water vapour by evaporation.
s: (a) The plain cup, because water collected in its tray while the waxed cup's tray stayed dry
(b) Evaporation, since its tray stayed dry (no seepage)
(c) 32 mL
(d) Wrong: 32 - 24 = 8 mL is not in the tray; it evaporated into the air

questions.q:
A Class 6 group in Patna keeps an open steel tumbler holding 200 mL of water in a locked cupboard in the lab for one week. Beside it they keep a steel bottle holding 200 mL of water with its lid screwed on tightly. The shelf under both stays dry all week, and nobody opens the cupboard. After the week the open tumbler holds 140 mL, while the closed bottle still holds 200 mL.
(a) How much water did the open tumbler lose?
(b) Asha says the water seeped out through the steel. Judge her idea using the evidence.
(c) Dev says nothing can disappear at room temperature, so someone must have taken the water. Judge his idea.
(d) What does the closed bottle add to this investigation?
(e) State where the missing water went and name the process.
questions.a: (a) 200 - 140 = 60 mL. (b) Not supported: the shelf under the tumbler stayed dry, and the closed bottle of the same steel lost no water, so the water did not seep through the steel. (c) Wrong: the cupboard was locked and never opened, and evaporation takes place continuously even at room temperature, so no heating or person is needed for water to disappear. (d) It is the same steel in the same place but its water cannot reach the air; since it lost nothing, the tumbler's loss must come from its surface being open to the air, not from the steel or the place. (e) The water changed into water vapour and went into the air of the cupboard; this is evaporation.
s: (a) 60 mL
(b) Rejects seeping: shelf dry and closed steel bottle lost nothing
(c) Rejects Dev: cupboard unopened, and evaporation goes on at room temperature
(d) Closed bottle shows the loss needs a surface open to air, not the steel or place
(e) Into the air as water vapour, by evaporation

questions.q: Drops of water collect on the inner side of a steel plate placed over a pan of boiling water. Which process forms these drops?
questions.a: Condensation: water vapour from the boiling water touches the cooler plate and changes into liquid droplets.

questions.q: Rekha takes a closed glass jar of chilled buttermilk out of the refrigerator and keeps it on the kitchen table. Within minutes the outside of the jar is covered with tiny drops. Where did the water in the drops come from?
o: Water vapour in the air around the jar
Buttermilk seeping out through the glass
Ice melting off the outside of the jar
Water vapour escaping from inside the closed jar
questions.a: Water vapour in the air around the jar: it came in contact with the cold surface of the jar and condensed into drops.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The reading of a digital weighing balance increases when a covered glass tumbler of water and ice cubes stands on it for 30 minutes.
Reason (R): Water from inside the tumbler seeps out through its walls.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false: the reading rises because water vapour from the air condenses on the cold tumbler and adds to the mass; marking the water level shows that no water seeps out.

questions.q:
Read the statements.
I. After a hot bath, the bathroom mirror gets covered with drops because water vapour from the hot water touches the cooler surface of the mirror.
II. Dew drops on plants form when water vapour present in the air comes in contact with the cold surface of the leaves.
III. Water vapour condenses into drops only on a container that has ice inside it.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only: drops form wherever water vapour touches a cold surface, as on the cooler mirror after a hot bath and on leaves as dew; III is wrong because leaves have no ice inside them, yet dew forms on them by condensation.

questions.q:
(a) What is humidity?
(b) Are rainy days more humid or less humid than other days?
questions.a: (a) Humidity is the amount of water vapour in the air. (b) More humid: the amount of water vapour in the air is more on rainy days.
s: (a) The amount of water vapour in the air
(b) More humid

questions.q:
Ayesha pours cold water from the refrigerator into a steel tumbler and leaves it on her desk for 10 minutes on two days. On a dry, clear day in February only a few tiny drops form on the outside of the tumbler. On a humid, rainy day in July the outside is soon dripping wet.
(a) Name the process that forms the drops.
(b) Explain why many more drops form on the rainy day.
questions.a: (a) Condensation: water vapour in the air turns into liquid drops on the cold surface of the tumbler. (b) Rainy days are more humid: the air holds more water vapour, so more vapour comes in contact with the cold tumbler and condenses into drops.
s: (a) Condensation of water vapour from the air on the cold tumbler
(b) Rainy air is more humid (more water vapour), so more vapour condenses

questions.q:
Ravi heats water in a half-filled pan and covers it with a steel plate. After a few minutes he lifts the plate and sees water drops on its inner side. His sister Mira says, "These drops are just boiling water that splashed up onto the plate."
(a) Name the process that formed the drops, and say what must happen to water vapour for it to take place.
(b) Where did the water vapour come from, and why does the plate act as the cooler surface?
(c) Ravi repeats this with water that is only warm, not boiling, so nothing splashes. Drops still form on the plate. Use this to judge Mira's claim.
questions.a: (a) Condensation: water vapour comes in contact with a cooler surface and changes into liquid water droplets. (b) The vapour came from the hot water in the pan, which was evaporating; the steel plate is cooler than the vapour rising from the hot water, so the vapour condenses on it. (c) Mira is wrong: drops form even when nothing splashes, so they come from water vapour condensing on the plate, not from splashed water.
s: (a) Condensation: vapour meets a cooler surface and turns into liquid drops
(b) Vapour from the hot water in the pan; the plate is cooler than the vapour
(c) Wrong: drops form without any splashing, so they come from condensed vapour

questions.q: A sealed plastic packet of frozen peas is taken out of a freezer and placed on a digital weighing balance in a kitchen. At the start the balance reads 500 g. After 20 minutes the outside of the packet is covered with drops and the balance reads 503 g. The drops are wiped off with a dry cloth and the balance reads 500 g again; the packet has no hole in it. (a) Find the mass of the drops. (b) Give two pieces of evidence that the drops did not come from inside the packet. (c) Explain where the drops came from and name the process. (d) Would drops form like this on a packet of dry peas taken from the kitchen shelf? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) 503 g - 500 g = 3 g. (b) The packet has no hole, so nothing can come out of it; and the total mass went up, which water moving from inside to outside could not do; after wiping, the packet is back to exactly 500 g, so it lost nothing. (c) Water vapour in the kitchen air came in contact with the cold surface of the packet and changed into liquid drops; this is condensation. (d) No: a packet from the shelf is not cold, and water vapour forms droplets only when it touches a cold surface.
s: (a) 3 g
(b) Two pieces of evidence: no hole, and mass increased (back to 500 g after wiping)
(c) Water vapour from the air condensed on the cold packet; condensation
(d) No, because the packet is not cold

questions.q:
At a wedding in Kochi on a May afternoon, a caterer keeps 40 glass bottles of lemon soda in a tub of ice. Each time a waiter lifts a bottle out, its outside is soon covered with tiny drops of water. Bottles of the same soda kept on a shelf in the hall, not chilled, stay dry outside. The weather report says that the humidity that afternoon was 88 per cent.
(a) Name the process that forms the drops on the chilled bottles.
(b) In which state was this water present in the air before it formed the drops?
(c) Why do drops form on the chilled bottles but not on the bottles kept on the shelf?
(d) What does the humidity of 88 per cent tell us about the air that afternoon?
questions.a: (a) Condensation. (b) As water vapour, the gaseous state of water. (c) The chilled bottles have a cold surface, and water vapour in the air forms droplets when it comes in contact with a cold surface; the bottles on the shelf are not cold. (d) The air held a large amount of water vapour.
s: (a) Condensation
(b) Water vapour (gas)
(c) Chilled bottles have a cold surface; shelf bottles are not cold
(d) The air held a lot of water vapour

questions.q:
Nikita wants to settle the 'lemonade mystery' in her class. She fills a steel tumbler with water coloured red with food colour, adds ice cubes made from the same red water, covers the tumbler with a steel plate and marks the water level with tape. The lab is at 35 °C. After 15 minutes the outside of the tumbler is covered with colourless drops, and the water level inside is still at the tape.
(a) Why are colourless drops evidence that the water did not seep out of the tumbler?
(b) Give one more piece of evidence from her set-up that nothing seeped out.
(c) Ira says pieces of the ice slipped out of the tumbler and melted on its outside. Judge her idea.
(d) Explain where the drops came from and name the process.
(e) Tara says condensation cannot happen in a lab at 35 °C because the air is hot. Judge her claim.
questions.a: (a) The water inside is red, so any water that seeped out would also be red; the drops are colourless. (b) The water level inside stayed at the tape, so it did not go down. (c) Not possible: the tumbler was covered by a plate, and the ice was made from red water, so melted ice outside would also be red. (d) Water vapour in the air of the lab came in contact with the cold outer surface of the tumbler and changed into liquid drops; this is condensation. (e) She is wrong: condensation needs a cold surface, not cold air; the tumbler's surface was cold because of the ice water, even though the lab was hot.
s: (a) Seeped water would be red; the drops are colourless
(b) The water level stayed at the tape
(c) Rejects Ira: tumbler covered and melted red ice would be red
(d) Water vapour from the air condensed on the cold tumbler; condensation
(e) Rejects Tara: the cold surface matters, not the air temperature

questions.q: Which of these is water in its solid state?
o: Snow lying on a mountain top
Dew drops on grass in the morning
questions.a: Snow lying on a mountain top: snow is frozen water, that is, water in its solid state; dew, steam and the mist on a mirror are tiny drops of liquid water.

questions.q: Which group contains only liquids?
o: Oxygen, carbon dioxide and water vapour
questions.a: Milk, oil and water: all three are liquids; stone, wood and glass are solids, and oxygen, carbon dioxide and water vapour are gases.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Ice and water must be different substances, because ice is hard and can be held in the hand while water cannot.
Reason (R): An ice cube left in a cup on a table gets converted into water.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true: ice turns into water, which shows that ice and water are two forms (states) of the same substance; feeling different does not make them different substances.

questions.q:
Read the statements about the states of water.
I. An ice cube moved from a square tray into a round bowl inside a freezer takes the round shape of the bowl.
II. Water poured on a clean, flat floor spreads out over it.
III. Water vapour from a boiling kettle stays close to the kettle and does not spread into the rest of the kitchen.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: II only: water flows and spreads on a surface. I is wrong because ice (solid) retains its shape whatever container it is placed in, and III is wrong because water vapour (gas) spreads out in the entire available space.

questions.q: Give one difference between ice and liquid water in (a) their shape, and (b) their ability to flow.
questions.a: (a) Ice keeps its own shape in any container, while water has no fixed shape and takes the shape of its container. (b) Water flows, while ice does not flow.
s: (a) Ice has a fixed shape; water takes the shape of the container
(b) Water flows; ice does not

questions.q: True or False? A cup of water poured into a large, empty closed box and the water vapour let into an identical box both spread out to fill the whole box. Give a reason.
questions.a: False. Water vapour (a gas) spreads out to fill the entire available space in its box, but the liquid water only spreads over the bottom of its box: it takes the shape of that part of the box and keeps its volume of one cup.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: only the water vapour fills the whole box; the water covers just the bottom, keeping its volume

questions.q:
Answer each part in one line.
(a) Name the state of water that flows and takes the shape of its container.
(b) Give two examples of solid substances.
(c) Give one example of a gas other than water vapour.
questions.a: (a) The liquid state (water). (b) For example, stone and wood (or glass). (c) For example, oxygen (or carbon dioxide).
s: (a) Liquid state
(b) Any two solids, such as stone and wood
(c) A gas such as oxygen or carbon dioxide

questions.q:
Three unlabelled samples are tested in a school lab.
Sample X: moved from a square box to a round dish, it keeps its square shape.
Sample Y: poured from a tall jar into a flat dish, it flows, spreads out and takes the dish's shape.
Sample Z: a little of this strong-smelling gas, let out of a small cylinder in one corner of a closed room, is soon smelled in every corner.
Name the state of each sample and the property that decides it.
questions.a: X is a solid: it retains its shape whatever container it is in. Y is a liquid: it flows and takes the shape of its container. Z is a gas: it spreads out to fill all the available space in the room.
s: X: solid, because it keeps its shape
Y: liquid, because it flows and takes the container's shape
Z: gas, because it spreads to fill the whole space

questions.q:
In the canteen of a school in Bhopal, the cook moves a block of ice from a rectangular steel box into a round plastic tub. She then pours 5 litres of milk from a tall can into a wide, flat tray so that it cools faster. Meanwhile samosas are frying, and their smell reaches the Class 6 room at the end of the corridor though nobody carries a samosa there. Her helper looks at the tray and says, 'The milk covers so much area now that it will easily fill 22 cups of 250 mL each.'
(a) What shape does the ice block have in the round tub? Why?
(b) What is the volume of the milk in the tray? Why?
(c) Which property of gases brings the smell of samosas to the classroom?
(d) Judge the helper's claim with working.
questions.a: (a) It stays rectangular: ice (a solid) retains its shape irrespective of the container. (b) 5 litres: a liquid takes the shape of its container, but its volume remains constant. (c) Gases spread out to fill all the available space, so the smell spreads through the air to the classroom. (d) The claim is wrong: 22 x 250 mL = 5500 mL, but the tray holds only 5 litres = 5000 mL; spreading out does not add milk, so it fills only 5000 / 250 = 20 cups.
s: (a) Rectangular, because a solid keeps its shape
(b) 5 litres, because volume stays constant
(c) Gases spread to fill all available space
(d) Wrong: 22 cups need 5500 mL but there is 5000 mL, enough for 20 cups

questions.q:
Raju measures exactly 400 mL of water in a measuring jug. He pours it into a tall jar, then into a flat tray, then into a round bowl, and finally back into the same measuring jug, which now reads 396 mL. He writes: 'Water does not keep its volume when it changes its shape.'
(a) What happens to the shape and the volume of water when it is poured into a different container?
(b) By how many millilitres did his reading fall?
(c) Give two likely reasons for this small fall that have nothing to do with a change of shape.
(d) Does his data support his conclusion? Explain.
(e) Suggest one change to his method that would give a fairer test of his idea.
questions.a: (a) Water takes the shape of the container, but its volume remains constant. (b) 400 - 396 = 4 mL. (c) Some drops were left sticking inside the jar, tray and bowl (or spilled while pouring), and a little water may have evaporated from the wide tray. (d) No: a loss of only 4 mL is explained by drops left behind and evaporation; it does not show that changing shape changes volume. (e) For example, pour slowly and let each container drain fully, use fewer pourings, or pour straight into one other container and back at once so that fewer drops are lost.
s: (a) Shape changes, volume stays constant
(b) 4 mL
(c) Two reasons: drops left behind or spilled, and evaporation
(d) No, the small loss is explained by those reasons
(e) One fair change: let each container drain fully, pour fewer times, or avoid the wide tray (less spilling and evaporation)

questions.q: A piece of butter put into a hot pan turns into a liquid. What is this change called?
questions.a: Melting: the conversion of a solid into its liquid state is called melting.

questions.q: In a kitchen, (P) a tray of water is kept in the freezer, (Q) a bowl of ice cubes is left on the counter, and (R) a bowl of hot liquid candle wax is left to cool on a table. In which of these is heat being removed from the substance?
questions.a: P and R only: the water in the freezer and the liquid wax that is cooling both lose heat and turn solid, while the ice on the counter is being supplied heat and melts.

questions.q:
Match each change in Column I with its example in Column II.
Column I: 1. Melting 2. Freezing 3. Evaporation 4. Condensation
Column II: P. Water left in an ice tray in the freezer becomes hard. Q. Drops collect inside the lid of a pot of boiling rice. R. The wax near the flame of a burning candle becomes runny. S. Wet footprints on the floor vanish after a while.
questions.a: 1-R, 2-P, 3-S, 4-Q: runny candle wax is melting, water becoming ice is freezing, vanishing footprints show evaporation, and drops inside the lid show condensation.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A chocolate bar that turned runny in a school bag on a hot afternoon sets hard again after an hour in the refrigerator.
Reason (R): A liquid changes into a solid when heat is removed from it, and this change is called freezing.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: the refrigerator removes heat from the runny chocolate, so the liquid changes back into a solid; this is freezing, even though it happens outside a freezer.

questions.q: Define (a) melting and (b) freezing.
questions.a: (a) Melting is the process of conversion of a solid into its liquid state. (b) Freezing is the process of conversion of a liquid into its solid state.
s: (a) Melting: solid changes into liquid
(b) Freezing: liquid changes into solid

questions.q: True or False? Liquid candle wax can be turned back into solid wax by cooling it. Name the change of state involved.
questions.a: True. Cooling (removing heat from) liquid wax changes it into a solid; this change is called freezing.
s: Verdict: True
Cooling removes heat and turns the liquid wax solid: freezing

questions.q:
Sana says, 'A freezer makes water into ice by putting coldness into it, while the sun melts ice by putting heat into it. So freezing and melting have nothing to do with each other.'
(a) What does a freezer actually do to the water placed in it?
(b) What happens to ice when heat is supplied to it?
(c) Is Sana's conclusion right? Explain.
questions.a: (a) It removes heat from the water, which then freezes into ice. (b) It melts and changes into water. (c) No: both changes depend on heat. Supplying heat turns a solid into a liquid (melting) and removing heat turns a liquid into a solid (freezing), so they are opposite changes linked by heat.
s: (a) The freezer removes heat from the water
(b) The ice melts into water
(c) Not right: both depend on heat, supplied for melting and removed for freezing

questions.q: On a summer afternoon, Meena sets up four things and leaves them for one hour: (i) an ice cube on a steel plate on the kitchen shelf; (ii) a small steel cup of liquid coconut oil, put into the freezer; (iii) a spoonful of liquid wax, just poured from a melted candle onto a steel plate on the shelf; (iv) a lump of coconut oil that had turned solid in the refrigerator, on a steel plate on the shelf. For each one, say what you would find after one hour, name the change of state, and say whether heat was supplied to it or removed from it.
questions.a: (i) Water: the ice melts, because heat is supplied to it from the warm kitchen. (ii) Solid coconut oil: the liquid oil freezes, because the freezer removes heat from it. (iii) Solid wax: the liquid wax freezes as heat is removed from it while it cools. (iv) Liquid oil: the solid coconut oil melts, because heat is supplied to it from the warm kitchen. The same coconut oil can melt or freeze depending on whether heat is supplied or removed.
s: (i) Ice melts into water; heat supplied
(ii) Coconut oil freezes into solid; heat removed
(iii) Liquid wax freezes into solid; heat removed
(iv) Coconut oil melts into liquid; heat supplied

questions.q:
A fish seller at a market in Visakhapatnam buys two ice slabs of 20 kg each at 6 a.m. She keeps slab A on her cart in the open sun and slab B in the shade of a tarpaulin. At 9 a.m. she weighs what is left: slab A has 11 kg of ice and slab B has 16 kg. She needs at least 8 kg of ice left at 3 p.m. to keep her last baskets of fish cold.
(a) Name the change happening to the slabs, and say whether heat is being supplied to them or removed.
(b) How many kilograms of ice did each slab lose from 6 a.m. to 9 a.m.?
(c) If each slab keeps losing ice at the same rate, how much ice will be left in each at 3 p.m.?
(d) Where should she keep her ice from tomorrow? Justify using (c).
questions.a: (a) Melting; heat is being supplied to the ice. (b) Slab A: 20 - 11 = 9 kg; slab B: 20 - 16 = 4 kg. (c) From 6 a.m. to 3 p.m. is 9 hours, three times the first 3 hours. Slab A would lose 3 x 9 = 27 kg, more than its 20 kg, so nothing will be left (it is all gone by about 12:40 p.m.). Slab B loses 3 x 4 = 12 kg, leaving 20 - 12 = 8 kg. (d) In the shade: only slab B still has the 8 kg she needs at 3 p.m., because in the sun more heat is supplied and the ice melts faster.
s: (a) Melting, with heat supplied
(b) A lost 9 kg and B lost 4 kg
(c) A: none left; B: 8 kg left
(d) Keep it in the shade, since only B meets the 8 kg need

questions.q:
Name the change of state in each event, choosing from melting, freezing, evaporation and condensation.
(a) An ice lolly left in the sun becomes runny.
(b) Mango juice poured into a mould and kept in the freezer becomes hard.
(c) Liquid ghee kept in the refrigerator becomes solid.
(d) Dew forms on the grass on a winter morning.
(e) A wet school bag left in the sun becomes dry.
questions.a: (a) Melting. (b) Freezing. (c) Freezing. (d) Condensation. (e) Evaporation.
s: (a) Melting
(b) Freezing
(c) Freezing
(d) Condensation
(e) Evaporation

questions.q: On which kind of day will washed bedsheets on a rooftop in Kanpur dry the fastest?
o: A hot, sunny and windy day
A cool, cloudy and still day
A rainy, humid day with no wind
A cool, cloudy and windy day
questions.a: A hot, sunny and windy day: sunlight and moving air both make water evaporate faster, and dry air does not slow it down.

questions.q: Arun has to dry a wet floor mat quickly. Which way will dry it the fastest, if everything else is the same?
questions.a: Spread flat in the sun: spreading it gives a larger exposed area, and sunlight makes water evaporate faster, so both help.

questions.q:
Match each observation in Column I with the condition in Column II that explains it.
Column I: 1. A towel spread out dries before a folded one. 2. Water in a bottle cap in sunlight dries before water in a cap in the shade. 3. Clothes dry faster on a windy day. 4. Clothes dry slowly on a rainy day.
Column II: P. More heat from sunlight. Q. More movement of air. R. Larger exposed area. S. More water vapour already in the air.
questions.a: 1-R, 2-P, 3-Q, 4-S: spreading out gives a larger exposed area, sunlight speeds up evaporation, wind is more movement of air, and a rainy day has high humidity, which slows evaporation.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Water in a bottle cap kept in sunlight evaporates faster than the same amount of water in an identical cap kept in the shade.
Reason (R): If the air already holds a lot of water vapour, water evaporates slowly.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: both caps are in the same air, so humidity does not explain the difference; the cap in sunlight gets more heat, which makes its water evaporate faster.

questions.q:
(a) Name two conditions that make water evaporate faster.
(b) Name one condition that makes water evaporate more slowly.
questions.a: (a) Any two of: a larger exposed area, more heat from sunlight (a hotter day), more movement of air (wind). (b) More humidity, that is, more water vapour already in the air.
s: (a) Any two: larger exposed area, sunlight or heat, moving air
(b) High humidity

questions.q: True or False? To find out whether sunlight makes water evaporate faster, Jaya puts 5 mL of water in a bottle cap in the sun and 10 mL of water in an identical cap in the shade. This is a fair test. Give a reason.
questions.a: False. In a fair test only one condition is changed and the others are kept the same; here both the place (sun or shade) and the amount of water are different, so she cannot tell which one caused any difference. Both caps should hold the same amount.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: two conditions are changed; the amount of water must be kept the same

questions.q:
A papad maker in Bikaner dries identical trays of papads in the same open courtyard on three days. The temperature is about the same and the air is still on all three days. She notes the humidity from the newspaper and the drying time.
Day P: humidity 30 per cent, 3 hours.
Day Q: humidity 55 per cent, 5 hours.
Day R: humidity 85 per cent, 9 hours.
(a) On which day did the air hold the most water vapour?
(b) What pattern links the humidity and the drying time? Explain it.
(c) She gets an urgent order on a day like Day R. Suggest one change, from this chapter, that would help the papads dry faster.
questions.a: (a) Day R, which has the highest humidity (85 per cent). (b) The higher the humidity, the longer the papads take to dry: when the air already holds a lot of water vapour, water evaporates slowly. (c) For example, use a fan to move air over the trays (more movement of air), or spread the papads out so more of their surface is exposed.
s: (a) Day R
(b) Higher humidity, longer drying time, because water evaporates slowly in humid air
(c) One valid change, such as a fan or spreading out more

questions.q: Plan a fair test, using two bottle caps of water, to find out whether moving air makes water evaporate faster. Write (a) the one condition you will change, (b) two conditions you will keep the same, (c) what you will measure, and (d) the result that would show that moving air speeds up evaporation.
questions.a: (a) Change only the movement of air: one set-up in front of a running fan (or in a breeze) and the other in still air. (b) Keep the same, for example: the amount of water, identical bottle caps (same exposed area), and the same light and temperature (both in shade, side by side). (c) Measure the time taken for the water in each cap to evaporate completely. (d) If the water in front of the fan disappears in less time than the water in still air, moving air speeds up evaporation.
s: (a) Changes only the movement of air
(b) Two correct conditions kept the same, such as amount of water and identical caps
(c) Measures the time for complete evaporation
(d) Fan set-up drying first shows moving air speeds evaporation

questions.q:
Anil, a farmer near Mandya, spreads his freshly harvested paddy (rice grain) in a thin layer on a cemented yard and lets it dry before he stores it. He dries an equal amount on three sunny days of about the same temperature. His notes say: Day 1, light breeze, humidity 40 per cent: dry in 6 hours. Day 2, light breeze, humidity 85 per cent: dry in 9 hours. Day 3, still air, humidity 40 per cent: dry in 8 hours.
(a) Name the process by which the paddy loses its water.
(b) How many hours longer did the paddy take to dry on Day 2 than on Day 1?
(c) Day 1 and Day 3 differ only in the movement of air. What made the paddy dry faster on Day 1?
(d) Day 1 and Day 2 differ only in humidity. Why did the paddy dry more slowly on Day 2?
questions.a: (a) Evaporation. (b) 9 - 6 = 3 hours. (c) The light breeze: with more movement of air, water evaporates faster. (d) The humidity was higher on Day 2, so the air already held a lot of water vapour, and water evaporates more slowly into such air.
s: (a) Evaporation
(b) 3 hours
(c) The breeze (more movement of air)
(d) Higher humidity: the air already held much water vapour, so evaporation was slower

questions.q:
A Class 6 group repeats Activity 8.7 with two liquids. They put 5 mL of water in a bottle cap (A), 5 mL of water on a plate (B), 5 mL of liquid hand sanitiser in an identical bottle cap (C) and 5 mL of the same sanitiser on an identical plate (D). All four are kept side by side on one bench, in the shade, with the fans off, and the time until no liquid is left is noted.
A: 150 minutes. B: 50 minutes. C: 30 minutes. D: 10 minutes.
(a) Which liquid evaporated faster? Support your answer with one pair of readings.
(b) For each liquid, how many times as fast did it evaporate from the plate as from the cap? Show your working and say what the two answers suggest.
(c) Kunal predicted that water spread on a plate would evaporate faster than sanitiser in a cap. Do the readings support him?
(d) The group repeats set-up C in front of a running table fan. Will it take more or less than 30 minutes? Give a reason.
(e) A nurse wants the sanitiser on her hands to dry as quickly as possible. Should she leave it as one drop in her palm or rub it over both hands? Use the readings to decide.
questions.a: (a) The sanitiser: for example, in identical caps the sanitiser (C) took 30 minutes while the water (A) took 150 minutes. (b) Water: 150 / 50 = 3 times as fast; sanitiser: 30 / 10 = 3 times as fast. Spreading out (a larger exposed area) made each liquid evaporate faster, by the same factor here. (c) No: water on the plate (B) took 50 minutes, but sanitiser in the cap (C) took only 30 minutes, so the sanitiser in the cap was still faster. (d) Less than 30 minutes: with more movement of air, a liquid evaporates faster. (e) Rub it over both hands: this spreads it over a larger area exposed to air, and the readings show the larger exposed area dried 3 times as fast (D 10 minutes against C 30 minutes).
s: (a) Sanitiser, with a correct pair such as C 30 min against A 150 min
(b) 150/50 = 3 and 30/10 = 3: a larger exposed area speeds evaporation of both
(c) No: B took 50 min but C only 30 min
(d) Less than 30 min, because moving air speeds evaporation
(e) Rub it over both hands: larger exposed area, as D (10 min) against C (30 min) shows

questions.q: High above the Earth's surface, the water vapour in cool air turns into tiny droplets. Around what are these droplets generally formed?
questions.a: Dust particles: the droplets that make up clouds are generally formed around dust particles.

questions.q: Why does water kept in a clay surahi stay cool in summer?
o: Water seeps through its surface and evaporates, which cools the water
Clay is always colder than the air around it
Its narrow neck stops the heat of the sun from reaching the water inside the pot
Water vapour from the air condenses inside it and cools the water
questions.a: Water seeps through its surface and evaporates, which cools the water: evaporation has a cooling effect.

questions.q:
Read the statements about clouds and rain.
I. As air moves higher above the Earth's surface, it becomes warmer and warmer.
II. Many small droplets in a cloud join to form bigger drops, and some become so heavy that they fall as rain.
III. Under special conditions, water from clouds may also fall as hail or snow.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: II and III only: droplets join into heavy drops that fall as rain, and under special conditions it may fall as hail or snow; I is wrong because air becomes cooler and cooler as it moves higher.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Drinking water stored in a stainless steel pot does not become as cool as water stored in an earthen pot.
Reason (R): Water does not seep through the surface of a steel pot, so there is no evaporation from its outer surface to cool the water.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: an earthen pot cools water because water seeps through it and evaporates; a steel pot lets no water through, so this cooling does not happen.

questions.q: What is the water cycle? Name the change of state that takes water from the Earth's surface up into the atmosphere, and the change of state that turns that water vapour into the droplets of clouds.
questions.a: The water cycle is the continuous circulation of water between the Earth's surface and the atmosphere: water evaporates as vapour and returns as rain, hail or snow. Evaporation takes the water up as vapour, and condensation turns the vapour into cloud droplets.
s: The water cycle is the circulation of water between the Earth's surface and the atmosphere
Evaporation takes water up; condensation turns the vapour into cloud droplets

questions.q: True or False? A balloon filled with a light gas and the water vapour above a lake both rise in the air for the same kind of reason. Give the reason.
questions.a: True. Both are lighter than air: the balloon contains gases lighter than air, and water vapour is lighter than air, so both rise.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: both the gas in the balloon and water vapour are lighter than air

questions.q:
Kiran wets her left hand with water, keeps her right hand dry, and holds both in front of a table fan.
(a) Which hand feels cooler?
(b) Explain why.
(c) She repeats this on a hot, very humid day in the monsoon and finds that her wet hand feels less cool than it did on a dry day. Suggest a reason.
questions.a: (a) The wet left hand. (b) The moving air makes the water on that hand evaporate quickly, and evaporation has a cooling effect; the dry hand has no water to evaporate. (c) When the air already holds a lot of water vapour, water evaporates slowly, so there is less evaporation and less cooling.
s: (a) The wet hand
(b) Fan speeds up evaporation, and evaporation cools
(c) In humid air evaporation is slow, so cooling is less

questions.q:
Near Thoothukudi, workers let sea water into a shallow salt pan until it is 10 cm deep. The floor of the pan is packed so hard that it lets no water through, and no rain falls during these hot, windy weeks. Each day the water level falls by about 2 cm, until only a layer of white salt is left on the floor. Months later, in the rainy season, rain falls on the hills inland and rivers carry it back to the sea.
(a) About how many days does it take for the 10 cm of water to disappear?
(b) Where does the water go, and by which process?
(c) Explain how such water can come back as rain over the hills.
(d) A visitor says the water that leaves the salt pans is lost for ever. Judge his claim.
questions.a: (a) 10 cm / 2 cm per day = 5 days. (b) It goes into the air as water vapour, by evaporation (the floor lets no water seep out). (c) Water vapour, being lighter than air, rises; higher up the air becomes cooler, and the vapour condenses into droplets around dust particles, forming clouds; the droplets join into bigger, heavier drops that fall as rain. (d) He is wrong: the water moves into the atmosphere as vapour, returns as rain (or hail or snow) and flows back through rivers to the sea; this continuous circulation is the water cycle, so the water is not lost.
s: (a) 5 days
(b) Into the air as water vapour, by evaporation
(c) Vapour rises, cools and condenses into cloud droplets, which grow and fall as rain
(d) Not lost: it circulates in the water cycle and returns as rain

questions.q:
Two cousins buy identical matkas from the same potter. Raghav lives in Nagpur, where the summer air is hot and dry; Sana lives in Mumbai, where the summer air is hot and very humid. On the same day, each fills a matka and a stainless steel pot with water at 34 °C at 8 a.m. and keeps them indoors. At 2 p.m. they find: Nagpur matka 24 °C, Nagpur steel pot 34 °C; Mumbai matka 30 °C, Mumbai steel pot 34 °C.
(a) By how many degrees did each matka cool its water?
(b) Why does a matka keep cooling its water only as long as water keeps seeping through its wall?
(c) Why did the Nagpur matka cool its water more?
(d) Sana says her matka must be of poor quality. Judge her claim using the data.
(e) Sana's mother suggests keeping the matka near a window where a breeze blows. Will this help? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Nagpur: 34 - 24 = 10 °C; Mumbai: 34 - 30 = 4 °C. (b) The cooling comes from the seeped water evaporating from the matka's outer surface; if no more water seeps through, there is nothing left on the surface to evaporate, so the cooling stops. (c) In dry air the water that seeps through the matka evaporates faster, and evaporation causes cooling; in Mumbai's humid air evaporation is slower, so there is less cooling. (d) Not supported: the two matkas are identical, from the same potter, and hers did cool the water by 4 °C; the smaller cooling is explained by the humid air, not by the pot. (e) Yes: with more movement of air, the water on the matka's surface evaporates faster, so the cooling effect increases.
s: (a) Nagpur 10 °C, Mumbai 4 °C
(b) Cooling comes from evaporation of seeped water; no seepage, no evaporation, no cooling
(c) Dry air lets water evaporate faster, giving more cooling
(d) Rejects the claim: identical pots; humidity explains the difference
(e) Yes: moving air speeds evaporation and so cooling

questions.q:
Answer each part in one line.
(a) What is the thin layer of air that surrounds the Earth called?
(b) What do the small droplets floating high in the air form?
(c) What do we call the heavy drops of water that fall from clouds?
questions.a: (a) The atmosphere. (b) Clouds. (c) Rain.
s: (a) Atmosphere
(b) Clouds
(c) Rain
